newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU hopes Blair win spells end for Euro-sceptics.
newsitem.headline: EU hopes Blair win spells end for Euro-sceptics.

text.p: Few tears were shed across Europe on Friday over John Major's thumping defeat in Britain's general election, which ended 18 years of Conservative rule and dealt a savage blow to British "Euro-scepticism".
But nor were Britain's EU partners kidding themselves that the advent of a new Labour government would mean a significant shift in Britain's stance on key issues of sovereignty.

EU diplomats said Labour could have an immediate impact at an inter-governmental conference (IGC) meeting on Monday -- expected to be the last before the Dutch EU presidency tables a draft treaty ahead of the Amsterdam summit in six weeks.

The IGC, due to complete its revision of the Maastricht Treaty by mid-June and streamline the bloc's institutions ahead of an ambitious eastward expansion, has seemed anathema to the Conservatives, who feared federalism and muttered darkly about the threat to the nation-state.

Monday's IGC agenda is tailor-made for Labour -- covering social policy, majority voting and relations with the European Parliament, all areas which the new government, in contrast to the Conservatives, can embrace.

"I think we'll see very early confirmation of a different attitude towards Europe," one diplomat said, adding: "It's fair to speculate that a new era in (British-European) relations will now open up."
Long viewed from the continent as a reluctant member of the European family, Britain is seen as having been largely negative throughout a stormy 24-year membership of the Union.
So often Britain, a proud island state, has gone it alone in Europe, totally at odds with its partners.

From mad cows to a single currency, from Europe's decision-making process to plans for a common defence, Conservative Britain has sounded a discordant note and at times revelled in glorious isolation, forever testing its partners' patience.
The Conservatives respond that the EU has adopted British views on trade and devolved decision-making and argue that being a partner does not always mean having to agree.
The IGC, in particular, has seemed anathema to a British government which feared federalism and muttered darkly about the threat to the nation-state.

Torn between the Euro-sceptics who abhor closer integration and a less vocal faction that sees a constructive European role for Britain, the Conservatives refused to contemplate surrendering the national veto on decisions they did not like.
They also opposed moves towards a common European defence policy and remained firmly outside the single currency club.
Europe hopes victorious Labour leader Tony Blair will usher in an era of cooperation in European affairs, but is not deluded that all will suddenly be well in cross-Channel relations.
"On key sovereignty issues -- money, borders and armies -- no one expects a change in the short-term," the diplomat said.
"But Europe has a pretty realistic attitude because Labour has been working very intensively behind the scenes and has made it very clear where it stands."
Blair will have the confidence of negotiating in Europe as head of a united administration, less distracted than Major and his need to deal with a sharply divided party, diplomats said.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette hailed Labour's win as a blow for "British Euro-scepticism", a view echoed by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl who said the result showed Britons did not like anti-European polemics.
"I would welcome it if Labour were more friendly towards Europe than the Conservatives were," Kohl said.
Robin Cook, likely to be Britain's new foreign secretary, has vowed that Labour will not threaten the EU with vetoes.
Labour is committed to the Social Chapter, ending a Conservative threat to block a new treaty if it had to bring in rules on working hours and continental-style works councils.

Labour is also more likely to move to Qualified Majority Voting (QMV) in some areas, but not on sensitive issues like taxation and security and, like the Conservatives, will stand firm on keeping control of Britain's immigration policy.
As in Britain, where an entire generation has grown up under Conservative rule, few in Europe can recall dealing with a pro-Europe Labour administration.

The last time Labour led Britain in Europe, the Shah of Iran was in flight as Ayatollah Khomeini returned to Tehran from exile, Leonid Brezhnev ruled the Soviet Union and, domestically, Britain's streets were hidden beneath mounds of rubbish during the "winter of discontent".
As the Amsterdam summit looms, Blair has little time to work his charm offensive, prove his European credentials and begin to unload Britain's Europhobic baggage.
